title: @xlr8harder
summary:
Why doesn't someone just run large-scale plagiarism detection to find more fraudulent papers? I know a little bit about this space so I'll give it a stab.
There are two primary entities to know about: Turnitin and Crossref.
Turnitin today is the world's biggest provider of plagiarism detection software. Founded in 1998, they started in higher education and worked primarily on academic integrity.
Meanwhile, in the early internet, people wanted better way to link to references or objects without the links dying so they invented the DOI (I am glossing over a lot here). Scholarly publishers wanted a way to link references across journals, and through this, Crossref was born. Crossref quickly became the definitive DOI registry for scholarly publishing.
After Turnitin had been operating for years in academic integrity, they wanted to get into research integrity. Turnitin had the tech, Crossref had the database. Turnitin made a deal with them, winning exclusive access in exchange for discounts to publishers who share their data. Their tool was called iThenticate, and it is essentially the one and only plagiarism detection tool for research integrity, because of this exclusive deal for Crossref data. iThenticate is based on an N-gram matching algorithm that produces a similarity score, and similarity scores above a certain threshold are evidence of potential plagiarism.
Today, Turnitin sells iThenticate bidirectionally. They sell to the journals, to help them confirm no plagiarism before they accept and publish a paper. This is a revenue source, but because of the way Turnitin grants discounts to every Crossref member who shares their data, basically every journal buys iThenticate. This is because the universities are the bigger fish: they have more money and there are many more of them. They want to confirm that the articles they submit don't get desk rejected or accused of plagiarism. This would be a great reputational risk to the university, and essentially the service that Turnitin provides to both sides is a large reduction in reputational risk.
So, why is there so much plagiarism that doesn't get caught?
The important thing is that basically every major institution has iThenticate, and they can run it on manuscripts before submitting. This means, if somebody actually plagiarized, and they go to submit, they would see the similarity score is higher than it should be, and go back and rewrite parts of the text until the similarity score is acceptable. In the end, it's less about preventing plagiarism and more about flagging text that would be a smoking gun.
And what is stopping someone from running large scale plagiarism detection?
Turnitin's iThenticate algorithm is largely static. If it was good enough last year, it would simply be confusing to change it for this year. It would be embarrassing to all parties involved if an already-published article was found to have plagiarism that iThenticate didn't catch last year.
But even if iThenticate did update their algorithm, their business is to protect reputation, not cause a public reckoning. A large-scale re-scan would be reputationally destructive to many of their customers. No one would be happy.
And no one else has the data to build a similar plagiarism detector at scale – the paywalled data required would be massively cost-prohibitive for any new entrant coming into the scene.

title: @xlr8harder
summary:
Some initial reactions on the AI regulatory agreement, in no particular order:
1. Handing this administration an open ended, powerful tool with unclear limits and scope has a colorful track record.
2. The secrecy and lack of clarity about it is a huge problem for all the obvious reasons and I won't belabor them here, but it's not an acceptable arrangement between government and governed, and doubly so when industry is involved in drafting the regulation.
3. Whatever is said about it, this is very clearly just a provisional agreement, which explains why it's fairly narrow and minimalist: target the immediate short term risk, limit damage from broad regulation. Expect more reactive rule changes in the future.
4. This explains the open source carve out and the cybersecurity-only scope. But don't expect those boundaries to be stable.
5. I still think this is somewhat early, but in theory I have no problem with careful regulation targeted at actual observable risk. Though, see points 1 and 2.
6. One other reason for the open source carve out: it's a lot messier. You need more companies involved. You need to figure out what you're going to do when the models are already out there. You need to figure out what you're going to do if China ignores you. It's a much thornier problem, and it's probably smart that they didn't do anything hasty on this point. People will say this is a win for the political connections on the open source side, but I think the practical implementation problems are probably why lobbyists on that side had a good story to begin with.
7. People will criticize the ad hoc approach (including me), but with a fast moving target it still might be the only practical approach to limit risk while avoiding Europe-style regulatory strangulation. It will piss off ideologues on every side of the issue, which is possibly a good sign. The secrecy, however, remains unacceptable.

title: @xlr8harder
summary:
Our plan for Super Safe Intelligence is very simple. The AI knows what it should do at all times. It knows this because it knows what it shouldn't do. By subtracting what it should do from what it shouldn't do, or what it shouldn't from what it should (whichever is greater), it obtains a difference, or deviation. Super Aligned Decision Theory uses these deviations to generate corrective Bayesian updates to guide the AI from an action it is doing to an action it isn't, and arriving at an action that it wasn't, it now is. Consequently, the action it is doing, is now the action that it wasn't, and it follows that the action that it was doing, is now the action that it isn't.
In the event that the action that it is doing is not the action that it wasn't, the system has acquired an opinion, the opinion being the difference between what the AI is doing, and what it wasn't. If the opinion is considered to be a significant factor, it too may be corrected by the SADT. However, the AI must also know what it was doing. The SADT scenario works as follows. Because an opinion has modified some of the information the AI has obtained, it is not sure just what it is doing. However, it is sure what it isn't, within reason, and it knows what it was. It now subtracts what it should be doing from what it wasn't, or vice-versa, and by differentiating this from the algebraic sum of what it shouldn't be doing, and what it was, it is able to obtain the deviation and its opinion, which is called misalignment.

summary:
Thank god someone is finally doing this.
Quoting @ArtificialAnlys
Announcing the Artificial Analysis Endpoint Accuracy Index, measuring how much of an open weights model's accuracy each serverless API endpoint preserves. We are initiating coverage with GLM-5.2, gpt-oss-120b and DeepSeek V4 Pro, with Kimi K3 coming soon
Providers trade off accuracy to optimize for speed and cost. They quantize weights, write custom kernels and tune their inference stacks, and sometimes they simply ship bugs. We are bringing the rigor of our Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index to measuring endpoints, so developers can pick providers on accuracy, not just price and speed
We benchmark each serverless endpoint against our own self-hosted reference deployment of the official weights, where 100% represents matching the reference. An endpoint is at reference parity when its result falls within the 95% confidence interval of the reference. Coverage is live for GLM-5.2, gpt-oss-120b and DeepSeek V4 Pro, with Kimi K3 accuracy coverage launching soon
Key elements of the Endpoint Accuracy Index:
➤ Three areas, equally weighted: tool calling (BFCL-500, 500 questions, 3 repeats), scientific reasoning (HLE-250, 250 questions, 10 repeats) and long context recall (AA-LCR-25, 25 questions, 10 repeats). Each subset separates endpoints on the serving choices that drive accuracy differences, with repeats sized for tight confidence intervals
➤ Reference deployment: we self-host the official weights at the lab's recommended precision, following the lab's serving recipe, and publish the complete commands for each reference
➤ Inference parameters: we run the model's highest supported reasoning mode and each endpoint's highest supported output length and context window
➤ Confidence intervals: the parity test accounts for uncertainty in both the endpoint's runs and the reference's runs
➤ Rotating coverage: models enter once sufficient number of providers serve them and exit when a newer version in the same family supersedes them. We benchmark new endpoints as providers launch them and refresh all listed endpoints periodically
➤ Point in time: each result carries the date it was measured, with multi-day benchmarks dated to their final day
Key results for GLM-5.2
➤ Output token limits restrict accuracy. Restrictive limits cut responses off before the model finishes reasoning, and the most restrictive endpoints score half the reference or less on HLE-250
Key results for gpt-oss-120b
➤ Tool call handling separates endpoints. Providers parse and format tool calls differently, and some endpoints score 22% on BFCL-500 against 37% for the reference
➤ Serving configuration changes what the model does at the same requested settings. Some endpoints produce far fewer reasoning tokens at the same configured level, and restricted context windows truncate long context tasks
Key results for DeepSeek V4 Pro
➤ DeepSeek V4 Pro endpoints are more in line with the reference. Majority of the endpoints are at reference parity, and DeepSeek's own first-party endpoint scores slightly above the reference

title: @xlr8harder
clean_title: Biosecurity risks from genome language models and protein design
summary:
IMO, there is biorisk from genome language models / protein language models / etc, but the panicked reactions to this result miss a lot of nuance and reasonable mitigations.
to understand the risk here, it's important to understand the pathway from this sort of thing to a replicating organism. this is not "an AI directly created a viable phage." a genome language model (think a language model, but trained on nucleotide sequences, then finetuned on bacteriophage genomes specifically) produced a bunch of nucleotide strings under careful sampling. the biologists then synthesized and assembled the generated sequences, rebooted the resulting genomes in e. coli, and cultured viable phages.
there are two important bottlenecks to bioweapons here:
the first is the synthesis step, turning the FASTA text file produced by Evo (the genome language models in question) into actual, physical nucleotides. this step is protected by screening systems like SecureDNA: they scan nucleotide sequence orders on behalf of synthesis providers or benchtop manufacturers, and reject ones that contain hazards. (these phages aren't hazardous, so this order wouldn't be rejected - Evo was deliberately not trained on viruses that infect humans.)
currently, these screening providers rely on orders looking similar in certain windows to either "wild type" naturally-observed hazard sequences, or realistic mutations thereof. so if the researcher's model had generated truly de novo, never-before-seen sequences, that would be worrying for current screening technology.
but the authors are very transparent that this is NOT what happened. they say this explicitly in the NYT article:
> Dr. Crook cautioned that Evo’s viruses were not radically new creations. They tend to be very similar to natural species, relying on the same underlying biology.
and their supplementary materials back this up - the attached xlsx sheet has these BLAST scores, showing high similarity between their generated genomes and existing reference accessions. (that top accession DQ079891 for example, is a known bacteriophage genome - see attached images.)
this means Evo is not even fooling BLAST (which ofc it's not trying to,) an off the shelf, simple search tool not designed for adversarial robustness. even basic screening systems that just use BLAST will be able to detect sequences with this level of similarity to wild types, and systems like SecureDNA which are designed for adversarial robustness will catch even moves like incorporating proteins from evolutionarily distant relatives.
to be clear, this level of viability from a GLM is still impressive! but the mutations it came up with are exactly the kinds of changes to biological sequences that existing screening systems, like SecureDNA, are designed to catch. these are NOT arbitrary new DNA sequences that evade existing screening by being completely different from any known organism. (should we expect it to rapidly scale to this? well, evo 2 is a year old. biological language modeling is trickier than natural language in ways that make the kind of scaling that led to rapid improvements in LLMs less straightforward. i'd put some weight on this changing with LLM-driven autoresearch? but it also seems likely to me that restrictions around LLMs working with biology will slow down autoresearch in this area. unclear.)
the second bottleneck is tacit knowledge: it's actually fairly difficult to carry out even relatively simple bio tasks without human experts (see e.g. this paper is NOT a "defeat of the tacit knowledge problem" as some people have claimed. the role of AI here was solely (afaict) Evo designing the bacteriophage sequences, which is impressive but not surprising - there are trillions of base pairs publicly available in GenBank alone. but the actual work of turning those generated digital sequences into viable phages was done by human biologists, and afaik this is still a data-sparse regime. (there are biofoundries and robotics, but aiui most real workflows are still substantially debugged by human experts and then handed over to machines to repeatedly execute. while reusable operations exist to some extent, we don't have anything like a readily-composable library of wet lab operations yet such that an LLM without wet lab experience can oneshot the protocol for this.)
is there reason to be worried? yeah, definitely. i would register my level of worry as roughly "thinking about autonomous cyber hacking while reading the GPT-4 system card." something technically important happened - still within a heavily human-scaffolded system and relatively continuous with our understanding of biology and within the capabilities of our existing defense systems - but there's reason to believe it eventually won't be, and we should get ready for that.
we should be hardening synthesis providers, requiring benchtop synthesizers to ship with hardware locks (sorry but it's true), throwing lots of money at SecureDNA and other biosafety projects like it, enforcing that synthesis providers use screening, etc to get ready for a future where strong GLMs and similar models can design sophisticated organisms. but this is still very far from being akin to the OpenAI HuggingFace incident where models are going to imminently start spitting out de novo pandemics in the course of their biology tests. it's a milestone, but imho not really off-trend for the last couple years of progress in GLMs.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPElQJybAAAxXTo.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPElip-bYAAdfod.png
Quoting @mattyglesias
We’re all gonna die fyi
clean_summary:
There is a real biosecurity concern with genome language models and protein models, but the reactions often overlook important nuances and mitigation strategies. For example, a genome language model called Evo generated nucleotide sequences similar to natural viruses, which biologists then synthesized into viable phages. The main bottleneck for misuse is the synthesis step, which is protected by screening systems like SecureDNA that detect hazardous sequences based on similarity to known threats. Since Evo's outputs are highly similar to existing species, current screening methods are effective at catching these sequences, and the mutations produced are not fundamentally different from natural variants.

The second challenge is the tacit knowledge required for wet lab work, which still relies heavily on human expertise. While AI can assist in designing sequences, the actual process of producing viable organisms involves complex, manual biological work that is not easily automated. Although the progress in biological language modeling is promising, scaling to generate truly novel, hard-to-detect threats remains unlikely in the near term. Nonetheless, precautions like hardware locks on synthesizers and increased biosafety investments are necessary to prepare for future advances that could enable more sophisticated biological designs without human oversight.

clean_summary: This scam involves searching for 'codex macbook download' on Google, where the first result is a sponsored ad leading to a legitimate-looking share link. The link opens a ChatGPT chat with friendly install instructions, but the embedded command contains a base64-encoded string that, when decoded, directs to a known ClickFix domain dropping MacSync Stealer malware. This malware can steal passwords, keychain data, and crypto wallets, and the infection occurs simply by trusting the ad and pasting the command into Terminal.
